e2ee.evidence: The server decodes and applies every Yjs update to its own document (Update::decode_v1) before persisting it, so it reads the content; the client-side AES-GCM covers only the offline IndexedDB copy.

postQuantum.evidence: Without end-to-end encryption, servers can read the data, so nothing protects it from a quantum computer either.

keysNotAccounts.evidence: Y-Sweet has no notion of users: the app's backend issues per-document client tokens after its own check, and "The endpoint should perform its own check to confirm the user is authorized to access the given document".

openSource.evidence: The server and the JS packages are under the MIT License ("Y-Sweet is MIT-licensed"), and the managed Jamsocket service was optional.

conflicts.evidence: Documents are Yjs CRDTs, so concurrent edits to text, lists and maps merge: "built on top of the Yjs CRDT library".
